ESKOM RECOVERY OR DEATH SPIRAL

By: Joy Summers | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
ESKOM'S RESULTS ARE BEING CLOSELY WATCHED BECAUSE WHAT HAPPENS AT ESKOM HAPPENS TO THE COUNTRY

Unique Selling Point:
THIS WEEK MINISTER LYNNE BROWN SUGGESTED THAT ESKOM MAY BE LYING TO HER ...DOWN THE RABBIT HOLE WE GO

Summary:
Reports and investigations, irregular spending and auditors blowing the whistle, bonuses and scandals, corruption, lack of corporate governance, multiple investigations and Junk status - you can find it all at our favourite electricity utility, Eskom. This week analysts and media are closely watching the latest results. Because what happens on Eskom's balance sheet impacts on us directly. Already the energy intensive user group is madly waving the red flag. Eskom's pricing is closing down businesses, but now they are running out of money and want to increase rates by 20% next year.

Further information:
The clock is ticking for scandal-infested Eskom as it readies to release its financial results amid confusion around the state firm’s true financial solvency.
Eskom’s financial results briefing is now scheduled for Wednesday after it was suddenly postponed two weeks ago. The question is if it will shed any light on whether Eskom is in good financial standing or not, amid a host of controversies that has plagued the institution.
Ministerial doublespeak
The doublespeak of Public Enterprises Minister Lynne Brown and Finance Minister Malusi Gigaba has done little to lift the fog.
Gigaba last week hinted that Eskom was on the verge of a bailout, while Brown recently insisted that Eskom was doing well.
Earlier this year Brown even said that Eskom was coping with its 2.2% tariff increase, which was much less than it had asked the national regulator for.
According to a leaked application, Eskom will ask for a 20% tariff hike next time around on the grounds that it won't be able to operate sustainably without collecting on that revenue. Yet last month, after Eskom’s annual general meeting, Brown reiterated that Eskom “recorded positive results according to its financial results presented to the AGM”.
She said Eskom was in a better financial position than it was a year and two years ago, at this time.
But over the weekend, Eskom refuted claims that it only has R20bn left in the kitty.
The Sunday Times, citing leaked financial statements, reported that the utility's current funds are only likely to last for the next three months and that Eskom may not be able to pay its 49 000 employees' salaries come November, unless it receives a bailout.
The Sunday Times report also suggested the postponement of Eskom’s results is to avert a crisis that would have required it to pay back R15bn owed to the Development Bank of Southern Africa (DBSA).
The DBSA granted that loan to Eskom in 2010, and Eskom has drained the facility. But one of the conditions in the loan is that it would be recalled if Eskom failed to achieve a clean audit, a disaster for the apparently cash-strapped state utility.
Eskom: No cash crisis
But Eskom on Sunday denied that it is facing a cash crisis.
"External auditors have confirmed Eskom is a going concern, and as a result the company sees these reports as being inaccurate and misleading," it said in a statement. "It is important to reiterate that Eskom is not facing any liquidity challenges, and that the company is confident that it will maintain sufficient liquidity to support its operations."
Eskom didn’t want to go into specifics, citing the limitations placed on disclosing financial information before the official announcement, scheduled for Wednesday.
The state utility however highlighted that Eskom’s financial position has always been supported by significant reliance on debt and borrowings. It said that as a result of its improved overall financial and operational performance over the last two years, it now has an improved balance sheet.
"Eskom also has sufficient government guarantees to execute its funding plan," it said."It has also maintained access to capital markets and raised committed funding."
Possible bailout
Hints of a bailout started surfacing last week at Gigaba’s media briefing on inclusive growth.
City Press reported that Gigaba's plan to revive the economy revealed that National Treasury intends to provide Eskom with “soft support”, which could mean a multibillion-rand bailout or increasing Eskom’s government guarantees to above R350bn.
Eskom was given a July deadline to submit to Treasury and the Eskom board a case for "soft support". 
Gigaba said at the briefing that details of a bailout will be unveiled as the process unfolds.
“What we are expressing is a deep appreciation of the weakening of the Eskom balance sheet,” he said.
“There is an urgency for us to provide assistance so that it is able to implement the capital build programme and fulfil its mandate. The Department of Energy will unveil what interim mechanisms are required in order to support Eskom until the next tariff application.”
Raising debt
With its governance crisis and despite still having the backing of government guarantees to the tune of R350bn, sources for funding are becoming more difficult to find. Government guarantees imply that Eskom can secure lenders, backed up by an undertaking from the South African government that it will honour any default.
South Africa has R477.7bn of guarantees available for public institutions. Of that, R308.3bn has been used. Information from Treasury indicates that Eskom is the biggest recipient, having used R218.2bn of the R350bn available to it by the end of the last financial year.
Chief financial officer Anoj Singh said that Eskom’s debt is expected to peak at R500bn.
• READ: Eskom to borrow R50bn a year in debt financing - analyst
Singh said international roadshows indicated there is still a significant appetite from international investors for Eskom’s bonds, despite the scandals and governance crisis around the company.
Singh believes the bond market could deliver up to $1.5bn (R19.78bn) in funding to bring Eskom to its financing target. But he said that going forward, the state enterprise would rely significantly on developmental financial institutions such as the China Development Bank.
"We'll rely on them for around 45% to 50% for our finance needs," he said. He added that Eskom expects 10% of its funds to be raised from international bond markets. 
If Eskom receives another bailout, it will be the second in only two years after it received a R23bn government bailout in 2015 to fix rolling blackouts that were plaguing South Africa at that stage.

Press Release:


Eskom: in recovery or death spiral?
Reports and investigations, irregular spending and auditors blowing the whistle, bonuses and scandals, a lack of corporate governance, and Junk status - you
can find it all at electricity utility, Eskom. This week analysts and media are closely watching their latest financial results because what happens on Eskom's
balance sheet, impacts the consumer directly. Carte Blanche asks: what does the future hold for the embattled power utility?

Script:


Eskom Results final script 2017 for TX Sunday 23rd July

Commentary One Zethembe Khoza- interim chairman
It was the best of times, it was the worst of times, said acting Eskom chairman Zethembe Khoza on Wednesday as he assured journalists that scandal hit Eskom, would restore its reputation

Zethemba Khoza
We remain resolute to restore this jewel – failure is not an option

Link
In many ways Eskom serves as a kind of barometer for South Africa. What happens here often reflects what’s going on in the country. More than any other State- owned enterprise Eskom has proved to be the treasure trove at the centre of the state capture project

Commentary Two
Against this background, and stepping into the shoes of Brian Molefe, replaced by Matshela Koko, now facing disciplinary action, is acting CEO Johnny Dladla. After 21 days in the job, Dladla delivered the annual results to a group of skeptical journalists

Johnny Dladla interim group Chief Executive
There will be no decisions that are taken in some corners by some individuals without being debated and decided on by the executive committee

Commentary three
Eskom say generation performance has improved, their new build programme is delivering to plan, and financial liquidity and profitability has been restored.

Dladla
On cost savings, we achieved R20 billion against a target of R17 billion. 53 % of funding for 2018 was secured, looking into operational performance the generation plant performance from 71.1 % to 77.3 %

Commentary four
But journalists were unconvinced. A week before it had been reported that Eskom was running out of money, and down to their last R20 billion, that would only last till November.

Phillip De Wet
Gentleman may we please, as a nation have from each of you individually, a clear and unambiguous answer- is Eskom in financial distress as defined by the companies act?

Dladla
The answer is an emphatic No
Khoza
We are financially sound and stable


Commentary five
But the Eskom pitbull, Sikonathi Mantshantsha is unconvinced. You will find him revealing story after story on Eskom, from his desk at the Financial Mail.

Bongani
Sikonathi you have said Eskom is fast running out of money, they say emphatically not

Sikonathi
That’s a big lie. They admitted that the R20 billion cash they have is the absolute minimum they should have and that is only enough for three months

Commentary six
Eskom’s told investors this week, they had R38.5 billion rand available. But Mantshantsha remains dismissive of an Eskom turnaround

Sikonathi
What turnaround, there is no demand for the power. The only reason revenue going up is because of the prices for less and less power, and they are getting more and more money

Commentary seven
Financial analyst David Shapiro is concerned that Eskom’s lack of corporate governance has had a domino effect on the economy.

David
From the results POV they are bumbling along, things are deteriorating but they are not going to collapse. What is more concerning is the people that are running it, and also to raise the necessary money to keep them going – those are the big questions

Commentary eight
Another big question is how Eskom will manage its huge debt levels. Will they have to turn to government to bail them out? Energy analyst Chris Yelland

Chris
So…. Eskom CFO debt level will rise to peak at R500 billlion

Commentary Nine
Ten years ago, Eskom’s debt was only R30 billion rand. This year it has ballooned to R334 billion rand, an increase of 1013%. Much of that has been incurred on Medupi, Kusile and Ingula- Eskom’s large build projects that have all run over-budget and over time. But to service that debt Eskom spends R38 million rand a day. Eskom’s profits are also down to a billion rand

Chris Yelland
Bottom line is net profit after tax has decreased dramatically by 80%



Commentary Ten
To fund their shortfall, Eskom wants a 20 % increase next year - an amount the energy intensive users group who represent big industry, say is not sustainable. Dr. Tsakani Mthombeni

Dr Tsakani Mthombeni
Electricity costs account for, from 10 % to 50%, of operational costs, so we really have a diversity of sectors who may just not survive any unreasonable increases in the tariffs and it may just drive a few companies over the edge

Commentary eleven
Eskom say they want to cut costs. But it’s in the fine print of the financials that the bodies are buried. Outa’s Ted Blom has found R3 billion rand of unauthorized spending that Eskom chose not to mention at the results presentation

Ted Blom
The big issue that wasn’t discussed at the Wednesday presentation – that the auditors have a qualified comment on the financials, to the extent of R3 billion rand of irregular expenditure, of which they can find NO trace inside the accounting system of Eskom

Commentary Twelve
But the results simply couldn’t compete against Eskom’s serious transgressions of corporate governance. Journalists, in a fighting mood were tired of Eskom spin.

Up Sound Sikonathi
Mr Khoza can you tell us if you have ever taken a gift or a bribe from anyone
Khoza
On record, I haven’t accepted any bribe or gift from anyone
Sikonathi
Can you do the same Mr Dladla?
Dladla
I have never accepted any bribe from anybody

Commentary thirteen
That was always going to be an awkward question for chief Financial officer Anoj Singh. He has been fingered in the Gupta leaks which show that the Gupta’s paid for his trips to Dubai

Sikonathi
Please do the same Mr Singh – have you ever taken a gift or a bribe from anyone?

Anoj Singh
Thank you sir- I can go on record and say, I have not received a bribe of any sorts or taken a bribe from anybody as it relates to the gifts -I will submit a tell all document so let’s wait for that and see where that lands up. Thank you



Commentary Fourteen
Daily Maverick’s Pauli Van Wyk’s questions, were uncomfortable, but Singh didn’t bat an eyelid

Pauli Van Wyk - journalist Daily Maverick
I have in my possession invoices of the Oberoi hotel those include things like spa massages of R10 000. And how did it happen that just a year before in June 2014 opened a shelf company in Dubai and deposited 400 000 Duram into a shelf company for you?

Commentary fifteen
That is approximately R1.4 million rand

Anoj Singh
Thank you for the question - I am in the process of preparing a document that I will be sharing with the board, the minister and SCOPA relating to those matters so I ask that the board and media as well

Commentary Sixteen
There are several issues that Eskom management would surely love to just go away, and one of those must be the Gupta’s Tegeta purchase of the Optimum Mine. A year ago, we exposed how Eskom gave Tegeta over half a billion rand prepayment that helped them buy Optimum Mine. Thanks to the State of Capture report and the Gupta leaks, we now know a lot more. And on Wednesday Mantshantsha added another piece of the puzzle.

Sikonathi
You were the accounting officer, you signed the guarantee on December 27th 2015. Where you in Johannesburg or Dubai when you made the signature?

Commentary Seventeen
Only months before the Gupta’s bought Optimum Mine, Eskom had signed surety for R1.6 billion rand on behalf of Tegeta to Absa Bank.

Anoj Singh Press conference
The guarantee was issued and cancelled subsequently …the guarantee expired and was never drawn on

Commentary eighteen
But this public admission may yet come to haunt Anoj Singh

Sikonathi
Eskom is not a financial service provider it had no business to stand surety for Tegeta to buy Optimum.
Bongani
But they will argue that in the event it was never actually used
Sikonathi
That is not the point – the fact that you could break open someone’s safe and not take the money does not make it legal.
Commentary nineteen
But Did the chairman know about the guarantee?

Up sound
As chairman of the board tender committee as the director of this company – did you know of that and how do you please reconcile that with Brian Molefe statements that they will not support Tegeta in any way financially to acquire Optimum

Khoza
I don’t recall
I only heard it for the first time when you asked the questions

Commentary twenty
On Thursday, the DA announced they will press criminal charges against Singh. They believe he played a pivotal role in the Gupta’s capture of Eskom. And then there is that small matter called Trillion

Up Sound Khoza
Trillian was subcontracted to Mackenzie when Eskom was requested to pay them directly R495 million and MCKENZIE R900 million total R1. 4 billion

Commentary Twenty-one
Trillian is another Gupta linked company that had no contract with Eskom, subcontracted to management consultants Mckenzie, and somehow wangled it that Eskom paid them directly. To do exactly what, has not yet been established

Johnny Dladla
I asked for an independent review on that because I am asking myself questions as well

Bongani
Were you satisfied with the explanations around the Trillian matter?
Sikonathi
They have no answers other than we also don’t know how we paid Trillian R500 million rand
Bongani
But surely someone should have instructed for that R500 million to be paid
Sikonathi
That money didn’t just walk out of Eskom into Trillian account, someone sent it there. Singh himself admitted we don’t know why we paid them. There was no contract for Trillian

Commentary Twenty-Two
But instead of being censured by Eskom, both Singh and Brian Molefe have each received bonuses of R1.9 million and R2.1 million rand respectively.

Carol Paton
If you are so concerned about governance as you say you are why has Mr. Singh not been suspended so he could be investigated and the allegations around him cleared

Khoza
With the matters that were raised in our own environment there is nothing that warrant to the degree that he could be suspended

Bongani
What should happen to Anoj Singh now?
Sikonathi
Anoj Singh should be nowhere near Eskom. In fact he should be in court answering to the charges of the fraud that has happened at Eskom and Transnet
Bongani
And as we sit here they are getting bonuses?
Sikonathi
They are getting bonuses and giving themselves bonuses

Commentary twenty- three
In fact, Eskom spent R4.2 billion rand on bonuses in the last financial year, and even Mr. Matshela Koko who must now answer to a serious charge of conflict of interest, received a bonus of R1.5 million rand.

The END 12 04.

PROMO ONE
The Eskom annual financial results on Wednesday turned into a marathon session as journalists piled the pressure onto the Eskom executives

PROMO TWO
Anoj Singh – Eskom’s chief financial officer was grilled on Wednesday by Financial Mail’s Sikonathi Mantshantsha

Anoj Singh
Thank you sir, I can go on record and say I have not received a bribe or taken a bribe from anybody.

PROMO THREE
Eskom’s profits are down, their debts are up, but they say their turnaround plan is yielding positive results
Dladla
On cost- savings we achieved R20 billion against a target of R17 billion

The only reason revenue going up is because of the prices for less and less power, and they are getting more and more money Commentary seven Financial analyst David Shapiro is concerned that Eskom’s lack of corporate governance has had a domino effect on the economy. David From the results POV they are bumbling along, things are deteriorating but they are not going to collapse. What is more concerning is the people that are running it, and also to raise the necessary money to keep them going – those are the big questions Commentary eight Another big question is how Eskom will manage its huge debt levels. Will they have to turn to government to bail them out? Energy analyst Chris Yelland Chris So…. Eskom CFO debt level will rise to peak at R500 billlion Commentary Nine Ten years ago, Eskom’s debt was only R30 billion rand. This year it has ballooned to R334 billion rand, an increase of 1013%. Much of that has been incurred on Medupi, Kusile and Ingula- Eskom’s large build projects that have all run over-budget and over time. But to service that debt Eskom spends R38 million rand a day. Eskom’s profits are also down to a billion rand Chris Yelland Bottom line is net profit after tax has decreased dramatically by 80% Commentary Ten To fund their shortfall, Eskom wants a 20 % increase next year - an amount the energy intensive users group who represent big industry, say is not sustainable. Dr. Tsakani Mthombeni Dr Tsakani Mthombeni Electricity costs account for, from 10 % to 50%, of operational costs, so we really have a diversity of sectors who may just not survive any unreasonable increases in the tariffs and it may just drive a few companies over the edge Commentary eleven Eskom say they want to cut costs. But it’s in the fine print of the financials that the bodies are buried. Outa’s Ted Blom has found R3 billion rand of unauthorized spending that Eskom chose not to mention at the results presentation Ted Blom The big issue that wasn’t discussed at the Wednesday presentation – that the auditors have a qualified comment on the financials, to the extent of R3 billion rand of irregular expenditure, of which they can find NO trace inside the accounting system of Eskom Commentary Twelve But the results simply couldn’t compete against Eskom’s serious transgressions of corporate governance. Journalists, in a fighting mood were tired of Eskom spin. Up Sound Sikonathi Mr Khoza can you tell us if you have ever taken a gift or a bribe from anyone Khoza On record, I haven’t accepted any bribe or gift from anyone Sikonathi Can you do the same Mr Dladla? Dladla I have never accepted any bribe from anybody Commentary thirteen That was always going to be an awkward question for chief Financial officer Anoj Singh. He has been fingered in the Gupta leaks which show that the Gupta’s paid for his trips to Dubai Sikonathi Please do the same Mr Singh – have you ever taken a gift or a bribe from anyone? Anoj Singh Thank you sir- I can go on record and say, I have not received a bribe of any sorts or taken a bribe from anybody as it relates to the gifts -I will submit a tell all document so let’s wait for that and see where that lands up. Thank you Commentary Fourteen Daily Maverick’s Pauli Van Wyk’s questions, were uncomfortable, but Singh didn’t bat an eyelid Pauli Van Wyk - journalist Daily Maverick I have in my possession invoices of the Oberoi hotel those include things like spa massages of R10 000. And how did it happen that just a year before in June 2014 opened a shelf company in Dubai and deposited 400 000 Duram into a shelf company for you? Commentary fifteen That is approximately R1.4 million rand Anoj Singh Thank you for the question - I am in the process of preparing a document that I will be sharing with the board, the minister and SCOPA relating to those matters so I ask that the board and media as well Commentary Sixteen There are several issues that Eskom management would surely love to just go away, and one of those must be the Gupta’s Tegeta purchase of the Optimum Mine. A year ago, we exposed how Eskom gave Tegeta over half a billion rand prepayment that helped them buy Optimum Mine. Thanks to the State of Capture report and the Gupta leaks, we now know a lot more. And on Wednesday Mantshantsha added another piece of the puzzle. Sikonathi You were the accounting officer, you signed the guarantee on December 27th 2015. Where you in Johannesburg or Dubai when you made the signature? Commentary Seventeen Only months before the Gupta’s bought Optimum Mine, Eskom had signed surety for R1.6 billion rand on behalf of Tegeta to Absa Bank. Anoj Singh Press conference The guarantee was issued and cancelled subsequently …the guarantee expired and was never drawn on Commentary eighteen But this public admission may yet come to haunt Anoj Singh Sikonathi Eskom is not a financial service provider it had no business to stand surety for Tegeta to buy Optimum. Bongani But they will argue that in the event it was never actually used Sikonathi That is not the point – the fact that you could break open someone’s safe and not take the money does not make it legal. Commentary nineteen But Did the chairman know about the guarantee? Up sound As chairman of the board tender committee as the director of this company – did you know of that and how do you please reconcile that with Brian Molefe statements that they will not support Tegeta in any way financially to acquire Optimum Khoza I don’t recall I only heard it for the first time when you asked the questions Commentary twenty On Thursday, the DA announced they will press criminal charges against Singh. They believe he played a pivotal role in the Gupta’s capture of Eskom. And then there is that small matter called Trillion Up Sound Khoza Trillian was subcontracted to Mackenzie when Eskom was requested to pay them directly R495 million and MCKENZIE R900 million total R1. 4 billion Commentary Twenty-one Trillian is another Gupta linked company that had no contract with Eskom, subcontracted to management consultants Mckenzie, and somehow wangled it that Eskom paid them directly. To do exactly what, has not yet been established Johnny Dladla I asked for an independent review on that because I am asking myself questions as well Bongani Were you satisfied with the explanations around the Trillian matter? Sikonathi They have no answers other than we also don’t know how we paid Trillian R500 million rand Bongani But surely someone should have instructed for that R500 million to be paid Sikonathi That money didn’t just walk out of Eskom into Trillian account, someone sent it there. Singh himself admitted we don’t know why we paid them. There was no contract for Trillian Commentary Twenty-Two But instead of being censured by Eskom, both Singh and Brian Molefe have each received bonuses of R1.9 million and R2.1 million rand respectively. Carol Paton If you are so concerned about governance as you say you are why has Mr. Singh not been suspended so he could be investigated and the allegations around him cleared Khoza With the matters that were raised in our own environment there is nothing that warrant to the degree that he could be suspended Bongani What should happen to Anoj Singh now? Sikonathi Anoj Singh should be nowhere near Eskom. In fact he should be in court answering to the charges of the fraud that has happened at Eskom and Transnet Bongani And as we sit here they are getting bonuses? Sikonathi They are getting bonuses and giving themselves bonuses Commentary twenty- three In fact, Eskom spent R4.2 billion rand on bonuses in the last financial year, and even Mr. Matshela Koko who must now answer to a serious charge of conflict of interest, received a bonus of R1.5 million rand. The END 12 04. PROMO ONE The Eskom annual financial results on Wednesday turned into a marathon session as journalists piled the pressure onto the Eskom executives PROMO TWO Anoj Singh – Eskom’s chief financial officer was grilled on Wednesday by Financial Mail’s Sikonathi Mantshantsha Anoj Singh Thank you sir, I can go on record and say I have not received a bribe or taken a bribe from anybody. metadata.Summary: Reports and investigations, irregular spending and auditors blowing the whistle, bonuses and scandals, corruption, lack of corporate governance, multiple investigations and Junk status - you can find it all at our favourite electricity utility, Eskom. This week analysts and media are closely watching the latest results. Because what happens on Eskom's balance sheet impacts on us directly. Already the energy intensive user group is madly waving the red flag. Eskom's pricing is closing down businesses, but now they are running out of money and want to increase rates by 20% next year.
metadata.Further information: The clock is ticking for scandal-infested Eskom as it readies to release its financial results amid confusion around the state firm’s true financial solvency. Eskom’s financial results briefing is now scheduled for Wednesday after it was suddenly postponed two weeks ago. The question is if it will shed any light on whether Eskom is in good financial standing or not, amid a host of controversies that has plagued the institution. Ministerial doublespeak The doublespeak of Public Enterprises Minister Lynne Brown and Finance Minister Malusi Gigaba has done little to lift the fog. Gigaba last week hinted that Eskom was on the verge of a bailout, while Brown recently insisted that Eskom was doing well. Earlier this year Brown even said that Eskom was coping with its 2.2% tariff increase, which was much less than it had asked the national regulator for. According to a leaked application, Eskom will ask for a 20% tariff hike next time around on the grounds that it won't be able to operate sustainably without collecting on that revenue. Yet last month, after Eskom’s annual general meeting, Brown reiterated that Eskom “recorded positive results according to its financial results presented to the AGM”. She said Eskom was in a better financial position than it was a year and two years ago, at this time. But over the weekend, Eskom refuted claims that it only has R20bn left in the kitty. The Sunday Times, citing leaked financial statements, reported that the utility's current funds are only likely to last for the next three months and that Eskom may not be able to pay its 49 000 employees' salaries come November, unless it receives a bailout. The Sunday Times report also suggested the postponement of Eskom’s results is to avert a crisis that would have required it to pay back R15bn owed to the Development Bank of Southern Africa (DBSA). The DBSA granted that loan to Eskom in 2010, and Eskom has drained the facility. But one of the conditions in the loan is that it would be recalled if Eskom failed to achieve a clean audit, a disaster for the apparently cash-strapped state utility. Eskom: No cash crisis But Eskom on Sunday denied that it is facing a cash crisis. "External auditors have confirmed Eskom is a going concern, and as a result the company sees these reports as being inaccurate and misleading," it said in a statement. "It is important to reiterate that Eskom is not facing any liquidity challenges, and that the company is confident that it will maintain sufficient liquidity to support its operations." Eskom didn’t want to go into specifics, citing the limitations placed on disclosing financial information before the official announcement, scheduled for Wednesday. The state utility however highlighted that Eskom’s financial position has always been supported by significant reliance on debt and borrowings. It said that as a result of its improved overall financial and operational performance over the last two years, it now has an improved balance sheet. "Eskom also has sufficient government guarantees to execute its funding plan," it said."It has also maintained access to capital markets and raised committed funding." Possible bailout Hints of a bailout started surfacing last week at Gigaba’s media briefing on inclusive growth. City Press reported that Gigaba's plan to revive the economy revealed that National Treasury intends to provide Eskom with “soft support”, which could mean a multibillion-rand bailout or increasing Eskom’s government guarantees to above R350bn. Eskom was given a July deadline to submit to Treasury and the Eskom board a case for "soft support". Gigaba said at the briefing that details of a bailout will be unveiled as the process unfolds. “What we are expressing is a deep appreciation of the weakening of the Eskom balance sheet,” he said. “There is an urgency for us to provide assistance so that it is able to implement the capital build programme and fulfil its mandate. The Department of Energy will unveil what interim mechanisms are required in order to support Eskom until the next tariff application.” Raising debt With its governance crisis and despite still having the backing of government guarantees to the tune of R350bn, sources for funding are becoming more difficult to find. Government guarantees imply that Eskom can secure lenders, backed up by an undertaking from the South African government that it will honour any default. South Africa has R477.7bn of guarantees available for public institutions. Of that, R308.3bn has been used. Information from Treasury indicates that Eskom is the biggest recipient, having used R218.2bn of the R350bn available to it by the end of the last financial year. Chief financial officer Anoj Singh said that Eskom’s debt is expected to peak at R500bn. • READ: Eskom to borrow R50bn a year in debt financing - analyst Singh said international roadshows indicated there is still a significant appetite from international investors for Eskom’s bonds, despite the scandals and governance crisis around the company. Singh believes the bond market could deliver up to $1.5bn (R19.78bn) in funding to bring Eskom to its financing target. But he said that going forward, the state enterprise would rely significantly on developmental financial institutions such as the China Development Bank. "We'll rely on them for around 45% to 50% for our finance needs," he said. He added that Eskom expects 10% of its funds to be raised from international bond markets. If Eskom receives another bailout, it will be the second in only two years after it received a R23bn government bailout in 2015 to fix rolling blackouts that were plaguing South Africa at that stage.
